Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the sources gathered.

---

## Numbers 14:23–45 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

### v.23 — "…not one will ever see the land that I swore to give their fathers. None of those who have treated Me with contempt will see it."

God swears an oath that this generation will not enter Canaan. Gill notes that the Targums of Jonathan and Jerusalem understand this as a formal oath (cf. Heb. 3:11): God now swears that those who tempted Him and were disobedient "should not inherit it." The Pulpit Commentary observes that the Hebrew idiom ("if they shall see…") is a strong negative oath form, also cited in Hebrews 4:3.

**Key insight (traditional):** The language of "treated Me with contempt" (or "provoked me," "spurned Me") means their sin was not mere weakness but active despising of God Himself. The Bible.org commentary (Cole) notes that "spurned" is a strong word meaning to despise or hold in contempt.

- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Cole/Bible.org: https://bible.org/seriespage/24-tragic-consequences-unbelief-numbers-1411-45

---

### v.24 — "But because My servant Caleb has a different spirit and has followed Me wholeheartedly, I will bring him into the land he has entered, and his descendants will inherit it."

**Why is Joshua not mentioned?** Poole explains Joshua was not among the people but a constant attendant upon Moses, and as their future chief commander, he was not reckoned among the ordinary spies. Gill adds that Joshua is mentioned later at v.30. The Pulpit Commentary suggests the entire tribe of Levi (including Eleazar) may have been excepted from punishment since they had no representative among the spies and had been loyal since the golden calf incident — so Joshua's omission here is unremarkable.

**"Another spirit" / "different spirit":** Gill says this means "a spirit of faith, and of the fear of the Lord, of might and courage, of truth and faithfulness" — different from the cowardice, unbelief, and disobedience that ruled the other spies. Poole says Caleb "was a man of another temper and carriage, faithful and courageous, not acted by that evil spirit… but by the Spirit of God."

**Spurgeon's classic treatment:** Charles Spurgeon preached that Caleb's "different spirit" was "not only a bold, generous, courageous, noble, and heroic spirit, but the Spirit and influence of God which thus raised him above human inquietudes and earthly fears." He said: "The real way to make a new life is to receive a new spirit. There must be given us, if we would follow the Lord fully, a new heart, and that new heart must be found at the foot of the Cross, where the Holy Spirit works through the bleeding wounds of Jesus." This reflects the Reformed/Baptist emphasis on regeneration as the source of faithful obedience.

**"Followed me fully/wholeheartedly":** Gill renders this "hath fulfilled after me" — obeyed God's word of command by going after Him. Ellicott notes that Caleb was specifically promised Hebron (Josh. 14:6-14) and the mountainous country the Anakim inhabited. The phrase "his seed shall possess it" can also be rendered "shall expel it" (i.e., drive out its inhabitants), as the Targum of Onkelos and Jarchi interpret it.

**Wesleyan/Methodist perspective:** Whedon's Commentary emphasizes the contrast between Caleb's wholehearted following and the unbelief of the majority, but does not differ substantially from other Protestant readings on this verse.

- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Poole: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/numbers-14.html
- Spurgeon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/caleb-the-man-for-the-times
- Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-14.html
- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm

---

### v.25 — "Now since the Amalekites and Canaanites are living in the valleys, turn back tomorrow and head for the wilderness along the route to the Red Sea."

**Interpretive difficulty:** Ellicott notes "considerable difficulty" regarding the meaning and connection of the first clause. The word for "dwelt" (or "living") often refers to temporary sojourn or lying in ambush (cf. Josh. 8:9; 1 Sam. 25:13). Following Ibn Ezra, Ellicott suggests: "the Amalekites and the Canaanites are abiding in the valley" — i.e., lying in ambush waiting to attack. This provides a strong reason for the command to turn back: "do not fall into the snare which is laid for you."

Gill similarly explains that though these peoples' proper habitation was in the mountain (Num. 13:29), they had now come down and "sat in the valley" — in ambush. God in His goodness warned Israel of this danger.

Poole gives two interpretations: (1) as an aggravation of Israel's misery — being so near the land but forced to turn back; or (2) as a pragmatic warning — enemies were very near, and if Israel did not depart speedily they would be attacked without God's protection.

**Dr. Constable** (Evangelical/Dispensational): Since Israel wanted to return to Egypt, God sent them back toward where they had been. The instruction to march toward the Red Sea (Gulf of Aqabah) was a reversal of their journey toward Canaan.

- Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-14.html
- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Poole: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/numbers-14.html
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-14.html

---

### vv.26–27 — "Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, 'How long will this wicked congregation grumble against Me? I have heard the complaints that the Israelites are making against Me.'"

The Pulpit Commentary notes this is a separate communication from vv.20–25 — it is (1) spoken to Aaron as well as Moses, and (2) addressed through them to the people at large. The earlier reply was God's answer to Moses the mediator; this is God's reply to the rebellious cries of the people.

Gill notes that the Jews (Jarchi) understand "this evil congregation" not of the whole congregation but of the ten spies, from which they derive that ten men make a congregation — and they interpret "murmur against me" transitively as "cause to murmur against me." But Gill argues the whole people are meant, as v.28 shows. Poole says the phrase "How long shall I bear with" is a short, imperfect speech frequent in anger (cf. Ex. 32:32; Ps. 6:3; 90:13), with "pardon" or "spare" being understood.

Constable comments that when the Lord asked "How long?" He meant this was the end. The oath formula "As I live" (v.28) was the strongest denial conceivable — what He said next was irrevocable.

- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-14.html

---

### v.28 — "So tell them: As surely as I live, declares the LORD, I will do to you exactly as I heard you say."

Gill calls this "the form of an oath" as in v.21. What they had wished for — death in the wilderness (v.2) — God would now grant them. Poole: "As you wickedly wished you might have died in the wilderness… I will bring your imprecations upon your heads."

The Enduring Word (Guzik, Pentecostal/charismatic) comments: "It was as if God said to them, 'You didn't want it when it was offered to you, so now you will never have it.'" This is a sobering principle: God sometimes gives people what their rebellious hearts demand.

- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Poole: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/numbers-14.html
- Guzik/Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/

---

### vv.29–30 — "Your bodies will fall in this wilderness—all who were numbered in the census, everyone twenty years of age or older… except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun."

The Pulpit Commentary: "All that had been enrolled as the soldiers of the Lord, to fight his battles and their own, but had refused, and had incurred the guilt of mutiny." Those numbered for war (Num. 1) would now die without fighting the Lord's battles.

Guzik (Enduring Word) notes the grim irony: Israel had said "If only we had died in this wilderness!" (v.2) — now God granted exactly that. Constable lists the ironic reversals: they feared their children would die in Canaan → God preserves the children; they rejected Canaan → God gives it to their children; they feared dying in Canaan → God lets them die in the wilderness.

- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-14.html

---

### v.31 — "But I will bring your children, whom you said would become plunder, into the land you have rejected—and they will enjoy it."

Guzik (Enduring Word) quotes Allen: "Only their children—whom they claimed outrageously that God desired dead—would be able to enter the land." The people had used concern for their wives and children as justification for unbelief (v.3); God turned that argument on its head.

Bible.org (Cole): "They accused God of bringing them into the land so that their wives and children would become prey for the Canaanites. So the Lord solemnly declared… 'You accused Me of wanting to kill your children, but I will bring them into the land which you have rejected.'"

- Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Cole: https://bible.org/seriespage/24-tragic-consequences-unbelief-numbers-1411-45

---

### vv.32–33 — "As for you, however, your bodies will fall in this wilderness. Your children will be shepherds in the wilderness for forty years, and they will suffer for your unfaithfulness until the last of your bodies lies in the wilderness."

The Pulpit Commentary notes: "Your children shall wander. Literally, 'shall pasture.' It was not altogether a threat, for it implied that the Lord would be their Shepherd and would provide for their wants in their wanderings."

The "whoredoms" (KJV) / "unfaithfulness" (BSB) that the children would bear: The Pulpit Commentary interprets this as idolatry — "whoredom" had been used as a synonym for idolatry in its aspect of spiritual unfaithfulness (Ex. 34:16). The commentary asserts that Israel was guilty of idolatry in the wilderness (cf. Acts 7:42–43), and these idolatrous practices, carried on in secret, were a sore trial to the generation growing up among them.

Bible.org (Cole) emphasizes the sobering generational principle: the children suffered for their parents' unfaithfulness. While God does not condemn any person for parents' sins (Ezek. 18:20), the fall means parents' sins are visited on children (Exod. 34:7; Num. 14:18). Cole applies: "if you love your children, kill your sin!"

- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Cole: https://bible.org/seriespage/24-tragic-consequences-unbelief-numbers-1411-45

---

### v.34 — "In keeping with the forty days you spied out the land, you shall bear your guilt forty years—a year for each day—and you will experience My alienation."

Gill and others see here a principle of divine proportionality: a year for each day of the spies' unfaithful reconnaissance. Constable notes the 40 years included the two years already spent in the wilderness. Maarsingh (quoted by Constable) suggests the round number 40 may refer to a human lifetime — generally, everyone above 20 would die within a 40-year period since few lived past 60.

The Pulpit Commentary observes that while the connection between 40 days and 40 years has an arbitrary surface appearance, God chose it as a fitting correspondence to underscore the justice of the sentence.

**"My alienation" / "My breach of promise" (KJV):** The Pulpit Commentary explains the difficult phrase "ye shall know my breach of promise" — this refers to the annulling of God's promise to that generation, what the BSB renders "My alienation." It is God withdrawing His favorable presence and the promised gift.

- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-14.html
- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm

---

### v.35 — "I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will surely do these things to this entire wicked congregation, which has conspired against Me. They will meet their end in the wilderness, and there they will die."

God's final, unappealable word. Guzik (Enduring Word): The language "conspired against Me" / "gathered together against Me" shows God viewed their grumbling as active conspiracy, not passive weakness. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the word translated "congregation" here is the same used for the assembly of Israel — now called "evil."

- Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm

---

### vv.36–38 — "So the men Moses had sent to spy out the land… were struck down by a plague before the LORD… only Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh remained alive."

The ten unfaithful spies died immediately by plague. Jensen (quoted by Constable) says: "As an unmistakable evidence that God's word of judgment would be literally fulfilled, the spies, except Joshua and Caleb, at this moment were struck dead with a plague from the Lord."

Guzik notes the swift judgment on the leaders of the rebellion, while the broader sentence on the congregation would unfold over 40 years.

Spurgeon, preaching on Caleb, said: "The ten fell, smitten with plague, but Caleb lived. Blessed is the man who hath the God of Jacob for his confidence!" He applied this devotionally: "If any man shall experience special deliverances, Caleb is he. If he follows God fully, God will fully take care of him."

- Constable/Jensen: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-14.html
- Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Spurgeon: https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/caleb-the-man-for-the-times

---

### v.39 — "And when Moses relayed these words to all the Israelites, the people mourned bitterly."

The Pulpit Commentary says this mourning was genuine in emotion but not in substance — it was sorrow over consequences, not true repentance. Bible.org (Cole) calls it "superficial repentance," proven by their immediate decision to disobey God's command to set out for the wilderness and instead go up to take the land.

Guzik: "Israel's superficial, energetic repentance afterward could not undo the judgment because it lacked genuine conviction of sin."

- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Cole: https://bible.org/seriespage/24-tragic-consequences-unbelief-numbers-1411-45
- Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/

---

### v.40 — "Early the next morning they got up and went up toward the ridge of the hill country. 'We have indeed sinned,' they said, 'but we will go to the place the LORD has promised.'"

The Pulpit Commentary: "Wishing to anticipate the retrograde movement commanded by God (v.25)… The prospect of being taken at their own word, and being excluded from the land which lay so near, brought home to them a sense of their folly; but their repentance merely consisted in a frantic effort to avoid the punishment which their sin had incurred."

**Whedon's Commentary (Methodist/Wesleyan):** This verse introduces a key theological observation about the two opposite phases of unbelief: "Presumption and despair are two opposite phases of unbelief. Within less than one day the Israelites despaired of conquering Canaan with the assured alliance of Jehovah, and then presumed to enter upon its conquest though he had announced the withdrawal of his aid. The natural man, when exhorted to religious effort, first avers that he can do nothing, even with God's aid, and soon asserts that by his own good works he can save himself without God."

This is a distinctively Wesleyan emphasis on the human will oscillating between despair and presumption when not grounded in genuine faith.

Bible.org (Cole): "Outwardly, they profess to be obeying God by going in accord with Joshua and Caleb's report. But actually, they were disobeying what God had just pronounced in judgment against them."

- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Whedon: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-14.html
- Cole: https://bible.org/seriespage/24-tragic-consequences-unbelief-numbers-1411-45

---

### vv.41–42 — "But Moses said, 'Why are you transgressing the commandment of the LORD? This will not succeed! Do not go up, lest you be struck down by your enemies, because the LORD is not among you.'"

Moses had already received the command in v.25 to turn back; he knew the cloud, the visible token of divine presence, would not guide them (Ellicott). Gill adds the Targum of Jonathan: "the ark, and the tabernacle, and the cloud of glory move not," which was plain indication that the Lord would not go with them.

Guzik: "They tried to gain His blessings without Him, which is unbelief." Constable similarly notes: "The key to success would not be their military might or psychological power but their obedient trust in God."

Bible.org (Cole) draws the gospel parallel: "These self-willed Israelites are a picture of those who reject God's promise of salvation by faith in Christ alone and determine to get to heaven by their own way, trusting in their own ability."

- Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-14.html
- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/
- Cole: https://bible.org/seriespage/24-tragic-consequences-unbelief-numbers-1411-45

---

### v.43 — "For there the Amalekites and Canaanites will face you, and you will fall by the sword. Because you have turned away from the LORD, He will not be with you."

Gill explains that the Amalekites and Canaanites had either removed from the valley (v.25) or detached a party to defend the pass on the top of the mountain. Moses warned plainly: the Lord would not be with them because they had turned away from His word.

Constable: Moses sounded the ominous warning "the LORD will not be with you" — yet they went anyway. This is the definition of presumption: proceeding without God.

- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-14.html

---

### v.44 — "But they dared to go up to the ridge of the hill country, though neither Moses nor the ark of the covenant of the LORD moved from the camp."

The Pulpit Commentary renders this "they presumed to go up" (Septuagint: διαβιασάμενοι ἀνέβησαν). "Thus they added to an evil distrust in the power of God an almost more evil trust in their own power." The Pulpit rejects the idea that "unbelief" was the single cause of both errors — rather, "it was one of those many cases in which men seek to atone for a fault on one side by rushing into as great a fault on the other side."

Gill: "In a bold, audacious, and presumptuous manner; they attempted to go up… notwithstanding the remonstrances of Moses… but withdrawing themselves from God and his ministers, and lifted up in themselves, and confident of their own strength, ventured on this rash enterprise." The Vulgate Latin renders it "being darkened they went up" — either their understanding was darkened, or they went up while it was still dark.

The absence of the ark and Moses was "the plainest possible token that the Lord was not with them" (Pulpit). Poole adds that with Moses stayed "no doubt all the Levites, and the silver trumpets, and Joshua, and perhaps the bulk of the people."

- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Poole: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/numbers-14.html

---

### v.45 — "Then the Amalekites and Canaanites who lived in that part of the hill country came down, attacked them, and routed them all the way to Hormah."

Gill notes the Amalekites came down the hill and met the Israelites as they ascended. Whedon comments: "Discomfited — Literally, pounded into pieces. 'Chased you, as bees do,' Deuteronomy 1:44, that is, with great ferocity when exasperated."

**The name "Hormah":** The Pulpit Commentary finds this "extremely perplexing," especially since Deuteronomy 1:44 places it "in Seir" (Edomite territory). It may be a place named by anticipation from the later destruction of the Canaanites by Israel (Num. 21:3). Alternatively, Gill cites Jarchi that it was so called from this very destruction ("Hormah" = destruction/devotion), and some render it appellatively: "even unto destruction" (Targum of Jonathan).

The Pulpit Commentary further notes: "It is clear from this passage, and still more from the parallel passage in Deuteronomy 1, that the expedition was swiftly and ignominiously repelled and avenged." The Israelites were driven off the mountain, across the Wady Murreh, and cut down.

Guzik (Enduring Word) summarizes: "Israel hoped to conquer Canaan without God's presence and help… What seemed impossible to them with God became impossible to accomplish without Him."

- Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/numbers-14.html
- Whedon: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-14.html
- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/numbers/14.htm
- Guzik: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/

---

## Summary of Protestant Traditions on Key Points

**On Caleb's "different spirit" (v.24):**
- **Reformed Baptist (Spurgeon):** The "different spirit" is regeneration — "a new heart… found at the foot of the Cross, where the Holy Spirit works through the bleeding wounds of Jesus." He emphasizes that true following flows from a divinely given new nature. (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/caleb-the-man-for-the-times)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik/Enduring Word):** Emphasizes the Spirit's empowerment for faith and courage. Caleb's different spirit is the Holy Spirit producing bold faith in contrast to the cowardice of the flesh. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-14/)
- **Older Anglican/Puritan (Poole, Gill, Pulpit):** Generally see "another spirit" as a different temper and disposition — a spirit of faith, courage, and obedience — with the Holy Spirit as the ultimate source. The emphasis is less on regeneration-vs-empowerment debates and more on the moral contrast.

**On presumption vs. despair (vv.39–45):**
- **Methodist/Wesleyan (Whedon):** Draws a specific doctrinal point: "Presumption and despair are two opposite phases of unbelief… The natural man, when exhorted to religious effort, first avers that he can do nothing, even with God's aid, and soon asserts that by his own good works he can save himself without God." This reflects the Wesleyan emphasis on the will's bondage in unbelief. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/numbers-14.html)
- **Reformed/Evangelical (Pulpit, Cole, Constable):** Tend to unify both errors under "unbelief" — the Pulpit Commentary resists reducing both to unbelief, seeing instead a pendulum swing from one sin to its opposite. Bible.org (Cole) makes this a picture of salvation by works vs. grace: trying to gain God's blessings by self-effort without God's presence.

**On whether God's pardon (v.20) was genuine:**
- **Reformed (Calvin, cited by Cole/Bible.org):** God's forgiveness was not forgiveness unto eternal life but meant He was delaying judgment by not wiping them out on the spot. The covenant with Abraham would not be abrogated. (https://bible.org/seriespage/24-tragic-consequences-unbelief-numbers-1411-45)
- **Traditional Protestant (Pulpit, Gill, Poole):** The pardon was real for the nation as a whole — the nation would not die — but temporal judgment on that generation remained. The Pulpit Commentary compares it to 2 Samuel 12:13: "I have pardoned according to thy word — such power had God been pleased to give unto man, that at the intercession of the mediator a whole nation is delivered from imminent death."

---
